Taking Our Python Skills to the Next Level: Building a Game Together

Throughout our journey so far, we have explored the fundamental concepts of Python. We have studied its syntax, learned about basic data types, loops, and conditions. Now, it is time to apply this knowledge in a more practical setting. Programming in Python is not just about understanding theoretical concepts. It is also about utilizing these concepts to solve problems and create tangible outcomes. To practice and reinforce our Python skills, we will develop a game together: Tic-Tac-Toe. Tic-Tac-Toe provides an excellent opportunity for us to apply what we have learned. Through this project, we will see how different components of Python come together to form a complete application. If you are not familiar with this game, you can visit this website and give it a try.

So, let us begin this journey of game development. By the end, we will not only have a functional game but also a more profound understanding of Python programming.

import time  # Import the time module for controlling pauses in the game

# Initialize the game board as a 3x3 grid of empty spaces
def initialize_game_board():
    return [
        [' ', ' ', ' '],
        [' ', ' ', ' '],
        [' ', ' ', ' ']
    ]

# Print the game board in a more visual manner
def print_game_board(board):
    for row in board:
        print('|', end='')  # Prevent the next print from starting on a new line
        for item in row:
            print(item, end="|")
        print('')  # Print a newline to separate rows

# Get input from the player for where they want to place their mark
def get_player_input(player_number):
    print(f'Player {player_number} turn!')
    player_input_x = input(f'Player {player_number}, please input the row number (0, 1, 2): ')
    player_input_y = input(f'Player {player_number}, please input the column number (0, 1, 2): ')

    return int(player_input_x), int(player_input_y)  # Convert input to integers

# Update the game board with the player's mark (X or O)
def update_game_board(player_number, row_number, column_number):
    if game_board[row_number][column_number] == ' ':  # Check if the spot is empty
        game_board[row_number][column_number] = 'X' if player_number == 1 else 'O'  # Place the player's mark
        return True  # Move successfully made
    else:
        print('That spot is full. Please choose a different spot!')
        return False  # Move not allowed

# Check if a player has won the game
def did_player_win(player_number):
    mark = 'X' if player_number == 1 else 'O'  # Determine the player's mark
    # Check rows, columns, and diagonals for a winning combination
    return any([
        all([cell == mark for cell in row]) for row in game_board] +
        [all([game_board[i][j] == mark for i in range(3)]) for j in range(3)] +
        [all([game_board[i][i] == mark for i in range(3)])] +
        [all([game_board[i][2 - i] == mark for i in range(3)])]
    )

# Check if the game board is full (a tie)
def is_game_board_full():
    return all(cell != ' ' for row in game_board for cell in row)

# Main game loop
def play_game():
    global game_board  # Declare game_board as a global variable
    game_board = initialize_game_board()  # Initialize the game board
    turn = 1  # Start with player 1's turn
    while True:
        print_game_board(game_board)  # Print the current game board
        row, col = get_player_input(turn)  # Get player input for row and column
        if update_game_board(turn, row, col):  # Try to update the game board
            if did_player_win(turn):  # Check if the current player has won
                print_game_board(game_board)
                print(f'Player {turn} wins!')
                return  # End the game
            elif is_game_board_full():  # Check if the game board is full (tie)
                print_game_board(game_board)
                print('It\'s a tie!')
                return  # End the game
            turn = 3 - turn  # Switch between player 1 and player 2
        else:
            print('Please choose a different spot.')
        time.sleep(1)  # Pause for 1 second to make the game easier to follow

# Start the game
play_game()

Let's break down the Tic-Tac-Toe code and highlight all essential aspects that you need to understand:

import

import time
  • import: Used to include a module in your code. Modules are collections of functions and variables.
  • time: A built-in Python module for working with dates and times. Here, it's being used to introduce a delay.

Function Definition

def print_game_board(board):
  • def: A keyword to define (declare) a function.
  • print_game_board: The function's name.
  • board: The function's parameter, representing the game board in our case.

Variables and Data Types

game_board = [
    [' ', ' ', ' '],
    [' ', ' ', ' '],
    [' ', ' ', ' ']
]
  • Lists: The game_board is a list of lists (also known as a matrix).
  • Strings: Each ' ' is a string, representing an empty cell in our game board.

Loop Constructs

for row in game_board:
  • for Loop: Iterates over a sequence, such as a list or range.
while True:
  • while Loop: Keeps iterating as long as a condition is true. This is an infinite loop, which keeps running until forcibly stopped, or a break statement is executed inside it.

Conditional Statements

if game_board[row_number][column_number] == ' ':
    ...
else:
    ...
  • if, elif, and else: Used to test conditions and execute blocks of code based on whether those conditions are true or false.

Input and Output

player_input_x = input(f'Player {player_number}, please input the row number (0, 1, 2): ')

  • input(): A function to get user input. It always returns a string, which is why we often wrap it with int() to convert it into an integer.

Built-in Functions and Methods

  • all(): Returns True if all elements in a list are true. Example: all(cell != ' ' for row in game_board for cell in row) means "Check if every cell in the game board is not empty".
  • range(): Returns a sequence of numbers.
  • any(): Returns True if at least one element in a list is true.

Flow Control

  • return: Ends the execution of the function and "returns" the value provided to the caller.
  • break: Exits the current loop.
  • continue: Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next iteration.

Boolean Logic

if not updated_successfully:
  • not: A logical operator that inverts the truth value.
  • Other common operators include and and or.

As we conclude this lecture, I hope that this tutorial has offered a clear demonstration of how the foundational principles of Python can be utilized in tangible projects. It is essential to understand that while individual concepts might seem simple or isolated, their combined application can create something as engaging as a game.

Remember, learning to program is a journey. Each step, be it understanding a concept or implementing a machine learning pipeline, brings you closer to becoming proficient. Continue practicing, experimenting, and building. Each project will refine your skills further!
